papers.title: Dynamical Fingerprints of Rare-Event Transitions from Transition Corridors
papers.abstract: Rare transitions are central in science, yet their mechanisms are obscured by the high dimensionality of complex dynamics, a challenge particularly pronounced in biomolecules where rare conformational transitions underlie functional processes. A transition-conditioned dynamical fingerprint is introduced for a rare (A mathbin{text{--}} B) event, in which the transition-relevant subset is targeted rather than a global decomposition and the problem is treated dynamically. Within a selected transition corridor, barrier-crossing motion is extracted and microscopic players are ranked through a corridor-conditioned informativeness measure, after which the highest-ranked players are subjected to intervention tests of their transition leverage using the REST2 scaling scheme, metadynamics, and targeted mutation. Across three benchmark proteins, targeting these players facilitates basin-to-basin transitions while maintaining high fidelity to the prescribed transition corridor, providing handles for mechanistic analysis, enhanced sampling, control, and design.

papers.title: Unavoidable Disasters: the Hsp70 Chaperone Can Only Prevent Aggregation Over a Limited Time Span
papers.abstract: Cells must attain and maintain proper protein folding and avoid aggregation: this is a pervasive challenge across all domains of life. Molecular chaperones are central to this process, acting through mechanisms shaped by the free-energy landscapes of their client proteins. The impact of chaperones on client-specific kinetic and thermodynamic characteristics, however, remains poorly characterized. Here, we develop the CHAMPION70 computational model to perform kinetic simulations on the E. Coli Hsp70 chaperone system in the presence of client-protein folding and aggregation. Experimentally determined folding/unfolding/aggregation rate constants are taken into account. In the case of weakly aggregation-prone clients, CHAMPION70 predicts that Hsp70 prevents aggregation only over timescales approaching the average human lifespan (79 years). For strongly aggregation-prone clients, however, aggregation inevitably occurs starting from a few minutes, even at higher-than-physiological Hsp70 concentrations. Thus, the Hsp70 chaperone system merely delays, yet surprisingly does not eliminate, the onset of aggregation. Further, CHAMPION70 predicts that Hsp70 most effectively retards the aggregation of slow-folding, thermodynamically stable clients. In contrast, thermodynamically unstable clients remain engaged with Hsp70 for prolonged periods even when aggregation propensity is low, thereby consuming chaperone capacity and reducing the extent of productive folding. This outcome suggests that condensate formation by proteins containing disordered regions may serve to mitigate unnecessary Hsp70 engagement. In all, our results provide a quantitative framework for understanding how client-specific kinetic and thermodynamic properties shape chaperone activity and show that the Hsp70 chaperone system does not altogether prevent aggregation: it merely retards it.

papers.title: Bacterial-Mimetic Membranes Reveal Hopanoid-Associated Domain-Like Lateral Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Bacterial membranes are increasingly recognized as laterally heterogeneous assemblies whose local organization can regulate transport, stress adaptation, and interactions with membrane-active compounds. However, the physical principles by which bacterial lipid composition generates spatially distinct membrane environments remain poorly understood, partly because experimentally tractable models that reproducibly exhibit lateral segregation and permit quantitative characterization are limited. Here, we show that a multicomponent, hopanoid-containing bacterial-inspired membrane spontaneously self-organizes into laterally distinct physical environments that are consistently resolved in experiments and molecular simulations. Giant unilamellar vesicles prepared from a lipid mixture inspired by lipid classes found in hopanoid-producing bacteria, including Methylorubrum extorquens, exhibit stable micron-scale lateral segregation, which is independently reproduced in compositionally matched coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations. The resulting membrane environments differ in composition, packing, order, mobility, and mechanical properties. Hopanoid-associated domain-like regions are more condensed, more ordered, and less mobile, whereas PE-rich non-domain regions remain more laterally expanded and exhibit faster lipid diffusion. At the global level, the bacterial-inspired membrane displays greater bending rigidity than a fluid phosphatidylcholine reference, while ATR-FTIR measurements independently support increased lipid-chain ordering and denser membrane packing. Together, these findings establish that hopanoid-containing bacterial-inspired membranes can spontaneously generate coexisting physical environments whose distinct local properties collectively determine global membrane behavior. The resulting experimental-computational framework provides a quantitative basis for investigating bacterial-like membrane heterogeneity and how local composition, dynamics, and mechanics govern responses to membrane-targeting perturbations.

papers.title: Mechanical Fidelity of Fixed-Cell Traction Force Microscopy
papers.abstract: Cellular traction forces contribute to biological processes including cell migration and tissue morphogenesis. Traction force microscopy (TFM) is widely used to quantify these forces in living cells, but it remains unclear how well measurements after fixation reproduce the live-cell state. Here, we systematically evaluated fixation-induced changes by paired comparison of the same cells before and after fixation using different fixation protocols and substrate stiffnesses. Fixation largely preserved the spatial organization and direction of substrate displacements and reconstructed traction fields, whereas displacement, traction, and strain-energy magnitudes showed fixation-dependent changes. Among the protocols tested, glutaraldehyde (GA) provided the closest agreement with live-cell measurements, retaining up to 99% of displacement and traction magnitudes and strain energy. Paraformaldehyde-based protocols caused larger reductions in these quantities while largely preserving their spatial organization. These results show that fixed-cell TFM, particularly with GA fixation under the conditions tested here, can provide measurements close to the live-cell state and offers a practical approach for combining TFM with post-fixation fluorescence imaging in a multi-well workflow.

papers.title: Lateral Membrane Heterogeneity Shapes Antimicrobial Association and Convergent Mechanical Responses
papers.abstract: Bacterial membranes are laterally heterogeneous, creating local physicochemical environments that can shape interactions with membrane-active antimicrobials. However, whether this spatial organization only affects local drug association or propagates into collective membrane responses remains unclear. Here we show that lateral membrane heterogeneity shapes antimicrobial association while distinct molecular responses converge on a common loss of membrane mechanical stability. Combining coarse-grained molecular dynamics, giant unilamellar vesicle fluctuation spectroscopy and microfluidic trapping, we follow octenidine, chlorhexidine and polymyxin B from molecular association to vesicle-scale behaviour. All three compounds preferentially associate with domain-associated membrane environments, but differ in how this preference changes with loading and in their effects on lipid mobility. Despite these differences, all three shift the membrane toward a mechanically softer state, while increasing exposure accelerates loss of vesicle stability under flow. These findings identify lateral membrane heterogeneity as an active determinant of antimicrobial response and provide a physical framework for understanding membrane-targeting activity beyond bulk composition and membrane-averaged charge.

papers.title: FLASH radiotherapy drives intestinal regeneration via macrophage-derived WNT4 signaling and attenuated T-cell inflammation
papers.abstract: Ultra-high dose rate radiotherapy (FLASH-RT) reduces normal-tissue toxicity, yet how elevated dose rate improves tissue repair remains unclear. Here we combined whole-abdominal FLASH-RT and conventional radiotherapy (CONV-RT) in mice with single-cell transcriptomics, trajectory analysis, cell-cell communication inference, and in vivo perturbation experiments to define the intestinal repair ecosystem. Compared with CONV-RT, FLASH preserved Lgr5+ intestinal stem cells and Fabp1+ absorptive epithelial cells. Trajectory analysis showed that FLASH maintained stem-cell differentiation toward mature epithelial states enriched for fatty-acid metabolism. During a day-3 repair window, FLASH was accompanied by enrichment of Mrc1 macrophages, increased WNT4-associated signaling involving Fzd5Lrp5/6-expressing stem cells, and early transient {beta}-catenin activation. In vivo augmentation of Wnt4 signaling promoted crypt regeneration after CONV-RT. FLASH also reduced Tcf7 and Tbx21 CD4 T-cell populations and TNF- levels, consistent with attenuation of the pro-inflammatory CD4 T-cell response during intestinal recovery. Together, these findings indicate that FLASH-associated tissue sparing involves coordinated remodeling of regenerative and inflammatory immune states, suggesting that radiation dose rate influences not only initial tissue injury but also the immune microenvironment of subsequent recovery. Targeting this immune-stem cell crosstalk may provide a strategy to mimic FLASH-like radioprotection.

papers.title: Nucleobase-Specific Recognition of DNA by Protamine
papers.abstract: Protamines--arginine (Arg)-rich, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs)--replace histones to compact DNA in the sperm nucleus. While folded domains can bind DNA site-specifically, whether IDPs exhibit DNA-sequence specificity remains open. Here, we used all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to characterize protamine-DNA binding. Eight copies of salmon protamine (33 residues with 21 Arg) rapidly wrap around a 35-bp DNA molecule. In addition to salt bridges with DNA phosphates, Arg hydrogen-bonds with multiple nucleobases on both strands or the same strand. At the major groove, protamine prefers GC over AT by a 2.6-to-1 ratio, with guanine's O6 and N7 atoms as hydrogen-bond acceptors; the preference is especially strong at G-tracts. This selectivity reverses at the minor groove, where AT overtakes GC by a 2.1-to-1 margin. The net effect is a moderate bias for GC over AT in protamine-base interactions. Additional simulations with 20-bp DNA molecules and free-energy calculations reinforce these observations. For experimental validation, we designed DNA sequences with 0-40% GC content. Protamine-DNA mixtures form aggregates, with an increasing propensity at higher GC content and upon shuffling into G-tracts. This work demonstrates that IDPs can bind DNA in a nucleobase-specific manner, with implications for protamine-mediated transcription silencing and remodeling of paternal chromatin.

papers.title: Learning from Hi-C reveals nuclear dynamical reorganization in budding yeast across the cell cycle
papers.abstract: Hi-C contact maps provide population-averaged measurements of chromosomal contacts. Converting these measurements, however, into three-dimensional structures and associated dynamics remains an underdetermined problem. Existing approaches broadly fall into two classes. Data-driven reconstruction methods that infer either a consensus structure or an ensemble of conformations, but do not inform on chromosome dynamics. Physics-based models, which generate dynamical trajectories, but require prior assumptions about nuclear geometry, chromatin mechanics, tethering, or molecular interactions. Here, we bridge these approaches using the Full-Inversion Chromatin model, a data-driven whole-genome polymer framework that learns an effective force field directly from Hi-C contact probabilities, integrated with Serpentine, a tool to quantify contact-map discrepancies while accounting for differences in sequencing coverage and sparsity. This generates structural ensembles of chromosomes and effective chromatin dynamics. We apply this method at 5-kb resolution to Saccharomyces cerevisiae in G1, mid-S, S/G2, G2/M, anaphase, and quiescence. Without explicitly imposing the spindle pole body, centromere or telomere tethering, predefined chromatin states, or nuclear-envelope interactions, the inferred ensembles recover these major features of yeast nuclear organization. Importantly, although dynamical information is not used during model training, the resulting polymer trajectories reproduce the subdiffusive scaling and chromosomal variations of independently measured chromatin motion. The model further predicts heterogeneous mobility along chromosomes and a distinctive telomere-dependent dynamical organization. Thus, population-averaged Hi-C contacts contain sufficient information to infer not only three-dimensional genome organization, but also effective, locus-dependent chromatin dynamics.

papers.title: Elucidation of Sequence Constraints for Protein Folding on the Ribosome
papers.abstract: The pioneering round of protein folding on the ribosome is critical for the proper assembly and function of many proteins. Emerging evidence suggests some proteins sample distinct conformational intermediates during translation, which implies the mechanisms of cotranslational folding may impose specific constraints on protein sequence. To assess how folding on ribosome may shape mutational tolerance, we paired a fluorogenic arrest peptide sensor with deep mutational scanning to survey how 9,480 mutations modulate E. coli dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) folding on the ribosome in live cells. By controlling for differences in variant abundance, we assess how these mutations specifically impact the efficiency of DHFR folding on stalled ribosomes. Mutagenic trends are broadly correlated with computational estimates for the change in the free energy of the native fold, suggesting that the sequence constraints associated with late-stage folding on the ribosome are broadly similar to those of post-translational folding. However, a close inspection of mutagenic trends reveals that folding on the ribosome is vulnerable to perturbations of specific contacts within a central portion of the adenosine binding domain and the C-terminal {beta}-strands of the discontinuous loop domain. Some of these regions are known to retain structure in the context of conformational intermediates that form on and off the ribosome, while others appear to be specific to cotranslational interactions. Together, our findings highlight how the constraints of folding on the ribosome may constrain evolutionary sequence space.

papers.title: One high-order ion-coupling mechanism generates multiple SLC1A stoichiometries
papers.abstract: Human excitatory amino acid transporter 2 (hEAAT2) is a glial transporter that clears glutamate and aspartate from the extracellular space to terminate neurotransmission. When this essential role is disrupted, excess extracellular glutamate causes excitotoxicity and neurological disease. hEAAT2 transports amino acids into cells against their concentration gradients by coupling uptake to the co-transport of Na+ and H+, and counter-transport of K+. Substrate transport also activates a thermodynamically uncoupled Cl- conductance, whose significance is unknown. Here, to dissect the molecular mechanisms underlying coupled and uncoupled ion transport by EAATs, we leverage the tractable Drosophila melanogaster homologue dEAAT2, which transports taurine as well as glutamate and aspartate. By functionally characterising dEAAT2, we confirmed it has features of a canonical EAAT transport cycle, including an uncoupled Cl- conductance. However, it functions an ion-independent electroneutral exchanger, in stark contrast to its ion-coupled electrogenic human counterpart. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and computational simulations confirmed the inability of dEAAT2 to transport cations, but just two point mutations conferred Na+, H+, and K+ dependence, reconstituting the complex ion coupling profile of human transporters in the Drosophila exchanger. We also showed that dEAAT2 transports taurine in a complex with Cl-, bestowing a unique Cl--dependence on taurine transport, independent of uncoupled Cl- flux. Our findings show that ancestral exchangers in the EAAT family preserve the machinery to achieve complex ion-coupled transport, revealing the molecular basis of high-order ion coupling in hEAATs.

papers.title: Expression-System Biases Compromise the Functional Assessment of KCNH2 Variants and Clinical Risk Assessment
papers.abstract: Background: Functional characterization of KCNH2 variants is essential for assessing pathogenicity in long QT syndrome type 2. Because hERG channels assemble as tetramers, the relative expression of wild-type (WT) and variant subunits critically influences channel function and pathogenicity assessment. However, commonly used experimental systems may not reproduce the balanced allelic expression observed in heterozygous patients. Methods: Allele-specific KCNH2 expression was analyzed in two independent RNA-sequencing datasets from human left ventricular tissue. Using the dominant-negative T74R hERG variant as a model, we calibrated the relationship between WT-to-variant expression ratios and hERG current amplitude. Using automated patch-clamp electrophysiology, we compared 3 dual-expression strategies: internal ribosome entry site (IRES), P2A-linked tandem constructs, and dual cytomegalovirus promoter (dCMV) constructs. Co-electroporation of WT and variant plasmids in different ratios was the reference. Results: Allele-specific expression analysis supported balanced KCNH2 expression in human left ventricular tissue. At a 1:1 WT-to-T74R expression ratio, hERG current amplitude was reduced to 31.0% of WT, consistent with a dominant-negative mechanism in which incorporation of 2 or more T74R subunits renders the channel nonfunctional. All 3 dual-expression strategies produced substantial expression imbalances, with the first cassette consistently favored. IRES constructs showed the greatest asymmetry. P2A constructs partially improved expression balance but introduced an additional N-terminal proline in the second cassette altering T74R-associated trafficking and channel biophysics. The dCMV system also failed to achieve balanced expression, including after stable integration. Co-electroporation of separate WT and variant plasmids provided the most reliable means of controlling their relative expression. Conclusions: Commonly used dual-expression constructs do not reliably reproduce balanced WT and variant hERG expression, potentially distorting assessments of dominant-negative effects and variant pathogenicity. Co-electroporation of separate plasmids provides a robust approach for high-throughput functional phenotyping under heterozygous conditions, with implications for the interpretation of KCNH2 variants and potentially other genes encoding multimeric ion channels.

papers.title: Microenvironmental Fingerprint of Maturing Tau Condensates from Spectral and Lifetime Phasor Analysis of a Solvatochromic Dye
papers.abstract: Solvatochromic dyes respond to changes in their local environment through variations in both spectral properties and fluorescence lifetime. These responses arise from the excited-state behavior of the probe, but the sensitivity of each response to a given environment can differ. In this work, we developed a multimodal phasor-based framework for two-photon spectral and fluorescence lifetime imaging analysis. To validate the framework, we imaged the solvatochromic dye ACDAN in water, glycerol, and ethanol. ACDAN showed clear spectral differences among the three solvents, whereas its fluorescence lifetime separated water from both organic solvents but not glycerol from ethanol, indicating that the two observables respond differently to the same environmental change. We then applied ACDAN to a well-described model system, the maturation of liquid-liquid phase-separated condensates of the microtubule-binding, neurodegeneration-related protein Tau into later-stage assemblies. Across Tau samples incubated for 1, 4, and 48 h, a progressive decrease in the ACDAN spectral phasor angle {theta} and increase in its phase-derived lifetime {tau}P suggested increasingly restricted dipolar relaxation in the probe environment. Differences among condensates were apparent by 4 h, whereas pronounced spatial heterogeneity within assemblies was observed at 48 h. Lastly, we evaluated the multimodal framework on Tau assemblies labeled with the fluorogenic probe Thioflavin T. As expected, this dye predominantly sensed its environment through its fluorescence lifetime, with comparatively limited spectral changes, whereas ACDAN reported microenvironmental changes in both coordinates. Together, this framework combines spectral and lifetime descriptors to characterize changes in the fluorescence response across Tau assembly maturation while retaining their spatial distribution.

papers.title: FACT frees Ubp10 from nucleosome sequestration after rapid H2B deubiquitination
papers.abstract: Chromatin-modifying enzymes must engage their substrate, act on it and release it, but which step limits their turnover is unclear. Using three-color single-molecule fluorescence, we directly visualized the yeast deubiquitinase Ubp10 removing ubiquitin from H2B on individual nucleosomes. Ubp10 cleaved the mark within seconds of binding, without detectable DNA unwrapping, yet it did not let go: ~80% of nucleosomes remained bound after 45 minutes, and unmodified nucleosomes formed similarly long-lived complexes. Ubp10 turnover is therefore limited by release rather than catalysis. The histone chaperone FACT relieved this bottleneck by accelerating Ubp10-nucleosome dissociation. In living yeast, nuclear depletion of the FACT subunit Spt16 increased the slowly diffusing, chromatin-bound fraction of nucleoplasmic Ubp10. These findings identify FACT-dependent release as a likely mechanism for recycling Ubp10 on chromatin. More broadly, a nucleosome can sequester the enzyme acting on it, making enzyme release a step at which chromatin modification can be controlled.

papers.title: Dual-reporter assay for selective small molecule inhibition of expanded toxic huntingtin
papers.abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expansion of CAG repeats in exon 1 of the human huntingtin gene (HTT). The resultant pathogenic allele (mHTT) produces a mutant huntingtin protein (mHtt) containing an expanded polyglutamine tract. Because mHtt drives neurodegeneration while wildtype huntingtin (Htt) remains critical for regulation of gene transcription and cell survival, an ideal therapeutic would specifically downregulate mHtt expression while preserving Htt. Small molecules are attractive candidates for HD given their ability to penetrate the blood-brain barrier and amenability to oral dosing, but there remains no high-throughput platform that reports both efficacy and allele selectivity. Here, we present a bacterial assay in which exon 1 of HTT and mHTT, each fused to spectrally distinct fluorescent proteins, are co-expressed in the same cell, allowing simultaneous quantification of their expression in the presence of small molecules. This high-throughput assay isolates the effect of small molecules on huntingtin expression without confounding factors present in mammalian cells, such as endogenous Htt or human RNA-binding proteins. To validate this assay, we evaluated two previously reported CAG repeat binding compounds and used circular dichroism spectroscopy and cell-free protein synthesis to investigate their underlying mechanisms. Furamidine exhibited reproducible, sequence-dependent effects, altering the structural stability of HTT RNA and selectively decreasing the wildtype Htt expression (a selectivity profile opposite to what is therapeutically required). In contrast, myricetin did not affect HTT RNA stability and its decreased signal in the dual-expression assay was due to fluorophore artifacts. This highlights the importance of complementary workflows in distinguishing genuine modulators from reporter-specific artifacts. Collectively, these findings establish the dual-expression assay as a screening platform for CAG repeat-targeting small molecules and demonstrate the importance of determining which allele reported compounds preferentially affect.

papers.title: Engineering Nanobody Conformational Switches
papers.abstract: Conformational signaling is widely used in biology, but remains difficult to engineer into proteins. Here, we explore ligand-induced folding of nanobodies as a general strategy to generate conformational receptors for a broad range of target ligands. More specifically, we have generated partially unfolded nanobody variants that fold exclusively upon binding to their target ligand. To do so, we have introduced destabilizing mutations in the framework region, carefully tuning their stability while preserving molecular recognition. Given the high conservation of the framework across different nanobodies, this approach is broadly applicable to many other target ligands, which has enabled us to engineer conformational switches for three different important biomarkers and drugs: the pregnancy hormone chorionic gonadotropin, the cytokine tumor necrosis factor alpha, and the chemotherapy and immunosuppressant drug methotrexate. Another useful property of conformational signaling is that it can directly gate signal transduction, which we have leveraged to build an optical sensor for the quantitative detection of the pregnancy hormone in urine. Finally, conformational signaling introduces new mechanisms for the allosteric modulation of binding, which we have explored to control the affinity and dynamic range of the sensor. Our work thus establishes a rational strategy for engineering conformational signaling receptors with customizable properties and generalizable for many different target ligands.

papers.title: A Deformulating Multi-Attribute SEC Method for Simultaneous Quantification of Total RNA, Conjugated Antibody, and Free Antibody in Targeted Lipid Nanoparticles
papers.abstract: Targeted lipid nanoparticles (tLNPs) hold promise for improving cell- and tissue-selective delivery of therapeutic payloads but introduce analytical challenges associated with characterizing both encapsulated cargo and surface-associated targeting ligands within the same formulation. Conventional nucleic acid and protein assays can be affected by nanoparticle scattering, matrix interference, or a limited ability to distinguish conjugated antibody from free antibody. Here, we report an online deformulating size-exclusion high-performance liquid chromatography (SE-HPLC) method that enables simultaneous quantification of total RNA, conjugated antibody, and free antibody from 5 L of tLNP sample. Following injection, exposure to a mobile phase containing sodium dodecyl sulfate and isopropanol disrupts the nanoparticles, enabling chromatographic separation of RNA, conjugated antibody, and free (unconjugated) antibody while minimizing sample handling prior to analysis. RNA was quantified by UV260 detection, whereas antibody was quantified by UV280 or intrinsic fluorescence detection to maximize sensitivity. The method demonstrated linear response over the evaluated concentration ranges, spike recoveries of 88-122%, and precision below 5% relative standard deviation. Application to purified tLNP formulations demonstrated simultaneous assessment of total RNA and conjugated antibody content, while confirming the absence of detectable free antibody following purification. Together, these results establish online deformulating SE-HPLC as a practical multi-attribute analytical method for characterization of tLNPs, enabling concurrent assessment of total RNA concentration, conjugated antibody concentration, and free antibody concentration using standard HPLC instrumentation.

papers.title: Nanomechanical phenotyping uncovers a non-canonical smooth muscle-like hypercontractility program in lung squamous cell carcinoma myofibroblasts
papers.abstract: Myofibroblast-like cancer-associated fibroblasts (myCAFs) drive the stiff, tumor-promoting microenvironment, yet their mechanical phenotype in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains undefined. myCAFs from major NSCLC subtypes (lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC)) were examined combining atomic force microscopy and traction force microscopy with molecular and signaling analyses. LUAD-myCAFs displayed canonical myofibroblast features, including elevated stiffness, traction forces, ROCK-MYPT1 signaling, and -SMA-rich stress fibers. Unexpectedly, LUSC-myCAFs amplified these nanomechanical features despite reduced ROCK-MYPT1 signaling and comparable -SMA levels. Instead, they exhibited a smooth muscle cell (SMC)-like contractile program characterized by enhanced SM-MHC(MYH11) expression colocalized with -SMA, ERK1/2-RLC hyperactivation, and DNA methylation reprogramming including SMC-contractility regulators. LUSC-myCAF hypercontractility was linked with reduced proliferative capacity and smaller intratumoral vessel lumens, consistent with the low CAF density and enhanced hypoxia patterns reported in LUSC. SMC markers were enriched and associated with adverse outcomes selectively in LUSC, highlighting the relevance of SMC-like myCAFs in LUSC progression. These findings unveil subtype-specific myCAF programs in NSCLC, and identify -SMA/SM-MHC(MYH11) myCAFs as key determinants of tumor mechanics, providing a rationale for the survival benefits of antihypertensive drugs targeting SMC hypercontractility. Moreover, they demonstrate that nanomechanical phenotyping can uncover translationally relevant myCAF phenotypes invisible to molecular profiling.

papers.title: Frequency-Dependent Structural Responses of Amyloid-β Fibrils to Terahertz Pulses: A Nonequilibrium Molecular Dynamics Study
papers.abstract: The abnormal aggregation of amyloid proteins into fibrils is closely associated with several neurodegenerative diseases, highlighting the importance of developing effective strategies to modulate fibril structural stability. Here, we employed nonequilibrium molecular dynamics(NEMD) simulations to examine the effects of intense terahertz-to-mid-infrared pulses on three amyloid fibrils (2LMP, 2MXU, and 5OQV), focusing on the combined effects of pulse frequency and electric-field strength. Frequency scans from 0.5 to 60 THz in 0.5 THz steps revealed frequency-dependent losses of {beta}-sheet content, with several common response patterns in these fibrils. Comparisons at 2, 23, 33, and 50 THz showed that pulse-induced changes in secondary structure differed from those in high-temperature controls. Hydrogen-bond analysis showed that total hydrogen-bond counts could partially recover even as interchain hydrogen bonds continued to decrease, with distinct responses among representative chain pairs. We therefore propose a two-threshold electric-field framework for fibril disruption: Eth1 describes the onset of structural perturbation, whereas Eth2 indicates persistent structural loss after the pulse. This framework offers a testable approach for characterizing amyloid structural responses to external fields, although the underlying energy-coupling mechanisms, quantitative thresholds, and long-term recovery require further validation. These findings may provide a theoretical basis for exploring external-field-based strategies to modulate protein aggregation.

papers.title: Lysenin Induced Membrane Curvature on Erythrocytes and Nanoporous Mica Free Standing Membranes
papers.abstract: Beta porin toxins are virulence factors that oligomerize in host cell membranes, forming beta-barrel pores that permeabilize target cells, leading to osmotic imbalance, cell lysis, and immune evasion. Despite extensive research on beta-pore-forming toxins (PFTs), significant gaps remain in understanding their role as actors of large-scale supramolecular membrane remodeling. While beta-PFTs are traditionally viewed as passive cylindrical conduits, their biological efficacy is fundamentally tied to an evolved ability to structurally alter the host cell membrane. In this study, we combine erythrocytes, model membranes and a novel engineered nanopores on mica substrates. We overcome the limitation of traditional mica substrates and demonstrate that lysenin pores do not merely permeabilize the membrane; they curve it into rigid, dome-like supramolecular structures. Moreover, to gain biophysical insight beyond the standard membrane models which do not directly consider the membrane insertions, we propose a hybrid model combining the biophysical models and the architectural models of pendentive domes, where the intrinsic wedge-shaped geometry of the monomers is considered. Experimental mechanical assessment of the lysenins domes shows a non-linear mechanical of stiffness with respect the radius of curvature as predicted by our hybrid model. Collectively, our work suggests that the beta-PFTs induce membrane curvature by the assembly of wedges. Beyond their pore-forming function, this membrane-bending activity may represent an additional mechanism by which beta-PFTs interfere with host-cell membrane repair.

papers.title: Distributed Network Sensing as an Escape Strategy
papers.abstract: The response of a swarm of ants or birds, living tissue of cells, or a robotic swarm, to spatial signals from the environment as a whole is a fundamental challenge for these decentralized systems. A promising alternative is embodied distributed sensing and decision-making, so that local environmental cues directly shape coordinated reconfiguration, growth, or movement without centralized control. Fluidic networks offer a physical basis for such systems, yet existing implementations are predesigned and limited in their ability to process spatial information across extended systems. Here, we investigate how fluid transport networks enable environmental sensing and adaptive response using the slime mould Physarum polycephalum. By exposing Physarum vein networks to dynamic pH environments, we show that the organism's ability to respond to aversive stimuli is governed by its spatial extent and network connectivity. Above a certain size, organisms with network morphology reliably detect and escape harmful conditions by network reconfiguration, whereas disconnected or spatially confined organisms fail to respond. In environments with competing stimuli, network morphologies enable integration of spatial information and repositioning into favorable regions. We identify local contractions as a physical mechanism that drives fluid redistribution and converts local stimulation into system-level responses. Finally, we generate different morphologies using fluidic and electrochemical control, demonstrating large-scale adaptation to complex environments. These results establish distributed fluidic networks as a framework for integrated sensing and actuation, providing design principles for autonomous soft robotic systems in dynamic environments.

papers.title: Multi-scale biophysical modeling of fungal colony growth
papers.abstract: Fungal colony growth is shaped by the fundamental physical operating principles of hyphal elongation, branching, and anastomosis, which collectively organize into macroscopic foraging networks. While sophisticated 3D models utilizing adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) on high-performance computing architectures can explicitly capture these discrete cellular mechanics, their immense computational cost prevents their integration into predictive ecosystem simulators. Here, building upon the Biological Modeling and interface eXchange (BMX) framework, we combine high-fidelity discrete hyphal mechanics with an analytically tractable, stochastic traveling-wave surrogate (sBARE) to provide multiscale simulations of fungal colonies at a fraction of the computational cost. By leveraging demographic fluctuations at the advancing front, our framework uniquely resolves macroscopic parameter degeneracies, separating the directed forward drift of leading tips from their effective diffusion to capture the macroscopic signature of negative autotropism in 3D networks. Simulations reproduce experimentally observed traveling wave profiles and confirm that interior network density under replete conditions emerges as an invariant self-regulated by fusion. Furthermore, global sensitivity analysis reveals that expansion speed and network density are governed by largely disjoint microscopic parameters. We demonstrate that because the physics of hyphal growth permit networks that are both exceptionally fast and dense, the empirical trade-off between sparse 'explorer' and dense 'exploiter' strategies observed in nature is not a strict mechanical constraint, pointing instead to metabolic limits on local growth rules. Our mathematically tractable approach bridges exascale-level cellular mechanics with macroscopic wave dynamics, enabling the integration of trait-driven advective fluxes and carrying capacities into the spatial transport and reaction network schemes of large-scale biogeochemical models.

papers.title: FUSION PORE CLOSURE DETERMINES SUBQUANTAL KISS-AND-RUN SEROTONIN RELEASE FROM FULLY LOADED DENSE-CORE VESICLES
papers.abstract: During kiss-and-run exocytosis, a transient fusion pore opens, releases part of the vesicular quantum, and closes without full fusion. This report investigates two questions: first, whether dense-core vesicles undergoing kiss-and-run contain the same number of molecules as those undergoing full fusion; second, whether subquantal release results from pore closure or vesicle depletion. We analyzed amperometric recordings of extrasynaptic serotonin release from dense-core vesicles in cultured leech Retzius neurons. Full-fusion events released 91,585{+/-}34,428 molecules (n=14), whereas kiss-and-run events released 58,344{+/-}20,759 molecules, 64% of the quantum. We analyzed the biexponential dynamics of the filtered amperometric current using Ohmic equations for cylindrical and toroidal pores. Hydrated flux packing (HFP) independently estimated the minimum peak pore diameter from the number of hydrated serotonin molecules crossing the pore. Kiss-and-run peak diameters were 2.1 to 3.2 nm, corresponding to the passage of 4 to 10 hydrated molecules. The vesicular serotonin content of individual kiss-and-run events was estimated by a frozen pore extrapolation (FPE), in which pores were kept at the peak HFP diameter. FPE yielded 102,650{+/-}10,989 molecules per vesicle (n=15), similar to the quantum obtained by integrating full-fusion events. Therefore, kiss-and-run subquantal release did not reflect a smaller quantum. We then compared the decay of serotonin flux with that estimated through the frozen pore at its peak diameter. In every event, the flux decayed faster, reaching half its peak in 0.59 (0.23 to 0.95) of the time taken by the frozen pore flux. We conclude that subquantal release during kiss-and-run exocytosis is governed by fusion-pore closure rather than vesicle depletion.

papers.title: Quantum Entanglement as a Physical Determinant of Genomic Instability in TP53
papers.abstract: Abstract Mutations in the TP53 tumor suppressor gene are among the most frequent alterations in human cancers, but whether quantum mechanical effects such as DNA entanglement, influence mutation patterns remain unexplored. Here, we applied a coupled quantum harmonic oscillator model to compute von Neumann Entropy (VNE), a proxy for quantum entanglement, across the TP53 sequence. We found that known mutational hot spots exhibited significantly elevated VNE compared to non-hot spot regions, suggesting that local quantum coupling may reflect structural instability or altered repair accessibility. CpG sites, traditionally linked to methylation-driven mutability, did not exhibit elevated VNE, indicating that quantum properties captured by our closed model are distinct from classical biochemical mechanisms. While these computational results raise the possibility that quantum effects could contribute to genomic instability in TP53, we caution that the analysis is limited by the small number of validated hot spots (n=6) and lacks biological validation. our findings are exploratory and should be interpreted carefully. If confirmed in a larger, multi-gene studies with biophysical measurements, a quantum informed framework could open new avenues for predicting mutation hot spots and understanding cancer mutagenesis. We advocate for interdisciplinary efforts bridging quantum physics and oncology to explore these possibilities further.

papers.title: Organised streaming of cerebrospinal fluid in the human third ventricle
papers.abstract: Quasi-periodic pressure pulses associated with cardiac and respiratory activity generate reciprocating cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) motion in the human ventricles. Regular waves dominated by the cardiac cycle are overlaid with cycles of low-frequency respiratory waves, the latter to become stronger in forced breathing or even dominated by large successive flushes in NREM sleep. The present study investigates how such waves contribute to residual streaming within the human ventricles. Transient CFD simulations were performed in the third ventricle at varying parameters of frequency, stroke volume and wave-form asymmetry. Increasing the aqueduct peak Reynolds-number, either by small stroke volume and high frequency or large stroke volume at low frequency, transfers the flow from a reversible flow pattern to the formation of clear preferential pathways, alternating between the in- and outflow cycle. The resulting permanent streaming flux across the aqueduct relative to the mean oscillatory flow-rate, i.e. the dimensionless streaming ratio SR follows a rational saturation relation, SR [~] ReAq,peak/(C + ReAq,peak), demonstrating that increasing the peak aqueduct Reynolds number yields diminishing returns and bounds the relative contribution of residual inter-ventricular streaming. These findings demonstrate differences in hydrodynamic organisation in the third ventricle and highlight the importance of this organisation for intraventricular fluid exchange.

papers.title: Opposing Roles of Cholesterol and Cholesterol Sulfate in Proton Transfer and Diffusion at Membrane Interfaces
papers.abstract: Sterols are fundamental components of biological membranes that modulate membrane fluidity and organisation, yet their role in governing interfacial proton dynamics remains underexplored. Here, we elucidate how cholesterol (Ch) and cholesterol sulfate (ChS) regulate excited-state proton transfer (PT) and long-range proton diffusion (PD) using a complementary dual-approach experimental framework combined with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Using a membrane-anchored photoacid in small unilamellar vesicles, we demonstrate that Ch accelerates local PT dynamics in gel-phase phosphatidylcholine membranes by inducing a fluid, liquid-ordered phase. Surprisingly, ChS inhibits local PT despite its negative headgroup. MD simulations reveal this inhibition stems from deeper probe embedding within ChS containing bilayers and the reduced basicity of sulfate relative to phosphate. Conversely, solid-state electrical measurements on supported lipid bilayers show a stark reversal for long range proton conduction (lateral PD): ChS increases lateral proton conductance by 400 fold under controlled relative humidity, whereas Ch decreases conductivity. This divergence arises mainly because ChS supplies titratable sulfate charge carriers, whereas Ch dilutes key phosphate proton mediators that promote a percolating interfacial hydrogen bonding network without providing charge carriers. Our findings demonstrate that sterols exert scale-dependent control over membrane PT/PD, revealing how headgroup chemistry, membrane fluidity, and hydration synergistically govern bioenergetic proton dynamics.

papers.title: Structural Basis of Second-Generation HIV-1 Maturation Inhibitor Activity by Magic Angle Spinning NMR
papers.abstract: The CA-SP1 junction of HIV-1 Gag forms a six-helix bundle (6HB) within the immature Gag lattice, sequestering the CA-SP1 cleavage site. Maturation inhibitors (MIs), such as Bevirimat (BVM) and its analogs, are an emerging class of HIV-1 antiviral compounds that stabilize Gag maturation intermediates by interfering with CA-SP1 proteolytic processing. Here, we report the binding modes of a potent second-generation BVM analog with an extended scaffold, HRF-4467, in crystalline CACTD-SP1-NC11 assemblies with inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6), as determined by magic-angle-spinning solid-state NMR (MAS NMR) spectroscopy. The atomic-level structure reveals that HRF-4467 binds asymmetrically in the SP1-NC11 six-helix bundle and stabilizes its helical conformation in the immature lattice, in both the wild-type and the BVM-resistant SP1-V7A Gag variant. Additionally, in the presence of HRF-4467, IP6 adopts distinct conformations in the wild-type CACTD-SP1-NC11 and the SP1-V7A variant. Taken together, our results establish a molecular basis for HRF-4467's improved antiviral activity relative to BVM and suggest strategies for designing inhibitors with enhanced performance against MI-resistant HIV-1 variants for potential therapeutic use.

papers.title: Maximum Likelihood Localization Maps
papers.abstract: Single-molecule localization microscopy commonly reconstructs images from estimated emitter coordinates. We calculate maximum-likelihood localization maps (MLLM), a non-iterative approach that evaluates positional likelihood from measured data and a supplied point-spread function. The MLLM of each detected single molecule image is added into a final upsampled image representing the overall molecular probability map, preserving the positional likelihood structure and obviating separate coordinate-based rendering. MLLM calculation is noniterative, fast, supports any calibrated point-spread function, accounts for local background variation, supports two- and three-dimensional reconstruction, and can be calculated in parallel.

papers.title: siRNA/mRNA payload of lipid nanoparticles quantified using fluorescence microscopy and correlation spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have emerged as the most promising vectors to deliver nucleic acids to mammalian cells. Advanced delivery strategies involving multiple nucleic acid species require a reliable determination of RNA payload and LNP size. Here, we use total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS) to determine mRNA payload and siRNA/mRNA codelivered payload. Particularly, FCS proves to be a reliable method for payload determination, independently of fluorophore properties that can be altered during encapsulation. By varying the PEG-lipid fraction relative to the reference ONPATTRO formulation, we find that mRNA payload of enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) coding mRNA increases from [~]10 with LNP size according to a power law with an exponent 1.3. Cryogenic electron microscopy (Cryo-EM) reveals that in this case blebs occur more frequently in small LNPs. For siRNA/mRNA coencapsulation the siRNA fraction within LNPs exceeds that in the initial RNA mixture, suggesting that coencapsulation is competitive and constrained by nucleic acid diffusion. Together, our findings highlight the importance of particle size and encapsulation kinetics in controlling the loading and composition of RNA payloads in LNPs.

papers.title: hAM-pe soluble extract increases human keratinocyte HaCaT cell-line mobility in scratch assays
papers.abstract: We have studied the impact of human amniotic membrane (hAM-pe) on wound closing speed in a scratch assay of human keratinocytes (HaCaT). Though not without limitations, scratch assays are useful for studying collective cellular displacement as a model of wound healing. We show that the treatment is effective in decreasing the average time that the cells need to completely close the wound, in agreement with previous emph{in vivo} experiments. We developed an automated segmentation software, and verified that a linear fit, though not completely describing the wound edge dynamics, is a robust method for comparing treatments and control measurements. By tracking the individual motion of a subset of cells, we found that individual treatment does not cause an increase in individual speed enough to explain the effect of the treatment at the collective (wound edge) level. Instead, the mean squared displacement and numerical simulations of a simple model of interacting active Brownian particles support the view that the main effect of the treatment at the individual level is to increase the persistence of cellular motion.

papers.title: Amyloid stability and condensate material properties independently govern the hnRNPA2 condensate to fibril transition
papers.abstract: hnRNPA2 is a component of cellular membraneless organelles many of which contain RNA and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs). RBPs frequently contain low-complexity domains (LCDs) that can also assemble into amyloid fibrils. Fibrils isolated from patients with frontotemporal lobar degeneration contain ordered segments of these LCDs and disease-associated mutations can enhance the homotypic interactions that promote aggregation. Although previous studies have largely examined the condensate-to-fibril transition by altering condensate stability, how amyloid structure governs this process remains poorly understood. Here, we show that the hnRNPA2 LCD forms a reproducible fibril fold and by combining structure-guided thermodynamic profiling, peptide design, mutagenesis and in vitro characterization under conditions with (two-phase) and without (one-phase) condensates, we define the molecular determinants of its assembly. We identify an aromatic triad within the fibril core that controls fibril formation kinetics and thermodynamic stability. Mutational analysis further reveals that condensate stability and fibril stability are largely independent. Finally, microrheology linked reduced condensate viscosity to faster fibril formation, supporting a role for condensate material properties in regulating aggregation kinetics. Together, these findings support a model in which the condensate-to-fibril transition is governed by the interplay between a disordered ''fuzzy coat'' and a fibril-forming aromatic triad within hnRNPA2. This work provides a structural framework for understanding how condensates can transition into amyloid assemblies.
